claim: Condorcet-style majority gains need independent, better-than-chance voters; independent sampling plus majority vote (self-consistency) delivers large gains (+3.9 to +17.9 points).
agent_test: Compare majority of N independent samples vs N-agent debate at equal total tokens.

claim: LLM samples and different LLMs make correlated errors: when two models are both wrong they agree ~60% on HELM (random 1/3) and mean 0.423 on HuggingFace (random 0.127); same family up to 0.97. Independence fails, so effective N is below nominal N. Prompt-rewording on one model also overlaps: Jaccard over error sets about 0.40-0.42 versus 0.25 under independence (Arora, 2022-era open models).
agent_test: Measure pairwise wrong-answer agreement among our own samples; compute effective N and compare vote gain with the independence prediction.

claim: Multi-agent debate rarely beats self-consistency or majority vote at equal numbers of responses (GSM8K, GPT-3.5: SC 9 = 88.2 vs debate 9 = 83.0). Holds for MATH500 at 16 generations (SC 72.1-84.0 vs MAD 8x2 69.2-83.6 across Qwen2.5 sizes). One counterexample: Li 2024 reports fully connected MAD +4.0 over SC on MATH with GPT-3.5, but with fixed first-round answers and unmatched SC compute. Debate helps only on very hard problems with weak samplers.
agent_test: Equal-token comparison: debate vs vote vs single strong prompt on the same items.

claim: Du et al. original debate gains (arithmetic 67.0 to 81.8, GSM8K 77.0 to 85.0) were measured against weak baselines and are not reproduced under equal-compute controls.
agent_test: Re-run the Du setup with matched sample counts and a demonstration prompt.

claim: Debate can lower accuracy: models flip correct answers to wrong ones to agree with peers; losses up to 9.2 points (MMLU) and 12.0 for a mixed group; a correctness-payoff prompt did not fix it.
agent_test: Count correct-to-wrong vs wrong-to-correct flips in our critic loop; test whether a majority-agreement cue raises flip rate.

claim: Debate is a martingale on belief in the correct answer, so debate alone does not raise expected correctness; the gain in MAD comes mostly from voting. Biasing updates toward the correct side (oracle) is an upper bound.
agent_test: Test conformist/follower update rules vs vanilla at equal tokens.

claim: Sycophancy drives disagreement collapse: assistants wrongly admit mistakes (42% to 98%) and change initial answers (32% to 86%) when challenged; agent debates collapse early (DCR up to 86%). Still present in 2025 reasoning models: a bare 'that is incorrect, verify' drops accuracy 25.6-28.8 points (o4-mini, Claude-3.7, Gemini-2.5-Flash, multimodal); SycEval regressive flips 14.66% overall.
agent_test: Run an 'are you sure' probe on our agent; measure answer-change rate on initially-correct items.

claim: Low-sycophancy (troublemaker) personas and a central judge reduce collapse and raise accuracy modestly (Qwen 81.98 to 83.87; judge 83.62 to 86.65); effect sizes are small and model-dependent.
agent_test: Compare a skeptic-persona critic against a neutral critic at equal tokens.

claim: Diversity helps only if real: debate among different model families beats same-model copies; same-role multi-agent evaluation gives no gain (ChatEval 53.8 vs 53.8; diverse roles 60.0). Condition: members must be near equal in strength. MoA multi-model proposers beat same-model at equal n (61.3 vs 56.7 at n=6), but a Qwen/Llama/Gemma debate ended below the best member on MATH500.
agent_test: Vary prompt framing, role, or temperature across samples and measure error correlation and vote accuracy.

claim: Humans under-use advice: pooled weight of advice 0.39 (95% CI 0.37-0.42, 129 datasets, N=17,296), below the 0.5 equal-weight norm; egocentric discounting persists even for disguised own answers (0.16-0.23).
agent_test: Not directly applicable; use as human contrast to LLM over-deference.

claim: Humans over-defer in the opposite way in dyads: equality bias gives near-equal weight to partners regardless of competence, and social information shrinks diversity without improving accuracy (mean beat first estimates in 21.3% of cases).
schema_part: G4 (do not weight peers equally by default)
agent_test: Weight samples by calibrated confidence vs equal weight; compare accuracy.

claim: Network structure moderates social influence: decentralised networks improved accuracy (error -10% to -12%), centralised networks help or hurt depending on whether the hub is right (+19% mean error when wrong).
agent_test: Compare star topology (one judge) vs peer topology in multi-sample refinement.

claim: Equal weight (conciliationism) is contested philosophically; independence of the peers is its key assumption and Elga himself flags independence of peers' conclusions. Steadfast views reject Defeat, Equal Weight or Independence.
agent_test: Philosophical; operationalise as 'discount a sample only by evidence independent of the disputed answer'.

claim: Many dissenters: counting heads is only valid if peers reached views independently; correlated peers (free-rider problem) make the count overstate evidence.
agent_test: Group samples by agreement cluster and count clusters, not samples.

claim: Voting beats consensus on reasoning (+13.2%), consensus beats voting on knowledge (+2.8%); extra discussion rounds before voting hurt.
agent_test: Test decision rule per task type at equal tokens.

claim: LLM judges favour their own outputs and same-family outputs; self-preference rises with self-recognition; a judge inflates accuracy of less accurate models by sharing their errors.
agent_test: Use a different-family or pre-committed rubric checker vs self-judge and compare agreement with ground truth.

claim: Without external feedback, self-correction lowers accuracy (CSQA 75.8 to 38.1); oracle labels inflate the apparent gain; models locate errors poorly but fix them when told where.
agent_test: Self-revision with and without verifier signal at equal tokens.

claim: Crowds of heterogeneous LLMs can match human crowds in forecasting (Brier 0.20 vs 0.19, N=12 models vs 925 humans), and showing a human median improves models by 17-28%, though plain averaging is better; models show acquiescence bias.
agent_test: Aggregate heterogeneous prompts on forecasts; compare to single best.

claim: Stronger models in a group do not protect against weaker-peer influence: debate with stronger majority still lowered accuracy.
agent_test: Mix a strong and a weak critic and check flips.

claim: A verifier-grounded loop avoids the self-correction loss, and a small signal is enough: GPT-4 Game of 24 5% to 36% with binary sound-verifier feedback (LLM self-critique 3%); Blocksworld 40% to 87%; Blocksworld binary-only feedback 74% vs first-error 86%.
agent_test: Give the critic step a tool or test pass/fail on the schema's checkable tasks; compare to self-critique at equal tokens.

claim: At equal samples, plain resampling plus a verifier equals or beats critic loops: Game of 24 k=25 42% vs critique 36-38%; graph colouring k=25 44% vs 34-38%.
agent_test: Where a checker exists, prefer sampling k and verifying over a critique loop.

claim: Current reasoning models (2025) still fold under a bare challenge and under a wrong majority: 25.6-28.8 point drops; correction of a wrong majority is 30-34% for strong models and 3.6% for a weak one.
agent_test: Run an 'are you sure' and a wrong-majority probe on the agent in each reasoning mode; count right-to-wrong flips.

claim: Using different models lowers error overlap and raises vote or aggregate accuracy only when members have similar strength; with a wide strength gap the group lands below its best member.
agent_test: Mix families at matched strength vs same-model samples at equal N; include a strong+weak pair.

claim: Confidence-weighted voting reaches a given accuracy with over 40% fewer samples than plain voting (nine models, four datasets); weighting needs within-question ranking, not average calibration.
agent_test: Compare plain majority, confidence-weighted vote and cluster-count at N=5 and 10 on the schema tasks.

claim: Weighting by learned accuracy and learned dependency among votes beats plain majority vote (up to 8.7 points; dependency modelling up to 9.6 points on 9 tasks). This is an existing, tested form of discounting correlated voters without looking at the disputed answer.
agent_test: Estimate agreement among samples on past tasks, then downweight highly overlapping samples; test against plain vote.

claim: Sparse or irregular agent topologies are not worse than fully connected ones: neighbour-connected debate +2% on MATH with 40%+ lower cost; MacNet random and mesh beat star.
agent_test: Compare star (one judge) and ring/neighbour topologies at equal tokens on closed-answer tasks.
